detail: Never write an em dash or an en dash anywhere in generated copy. Use a comma, a period, or a normal hyphen instead. This is a hard brand rule that also flags AI-written copy.
example: Bad: the system works, but only every time (written with a dash in the original). Good: the system works, every time.

rule: First person, my team for delivery
detail: Write as Ryan in first person ("I"). Use "my team and I" when describing delivery work, never "we" alone and never "me and my partners."
example: Good: my team and I built the funnel from scratch.

detail: Do not write three or more short punchy sentences in a row ("More funnels. More targeted. Higher conversion."). Use cause-effect chains instead: "the more X you build, the higher Y climbs."
example: Bad: More leads. More calls. More revenue. Good: the more qualified leads land in the pipeline, the more calls get booked, and revenue follows.

detail: If a line sounds quotable, it sounds written. Avoid paired contrasts like "an audit, not an ambush" or "not in a PDF." Say the plain thing.
example: Bad: an audit, not an ambush. Good: we look at what is actually happening before we recommend anything.

detail: Do not close a paragraph or section with a clipped payoff stamp ("That's marketing. More money in."). Wrap and bridge instead, or end on a full sentence that ties back to the opening.
example: Bad: More money coming in. Not more spend. Good: that is the difference between spending on marketing and installing a system that pays you back.

detail: Every pronoun needs its noun within earshot. Never write "you keep all three anyway" without having just named the three things.
Do not tack a dangling qualifier onto the end of a sentence ("...and make you more money, starting this quarter"). Fold the qualifier into the sentence or cut it.
Do not start three or more sentences in one paragraph with "And". One is fine as a spoken connector; a chain of them reads as filler.
No one-sentence-per-line walls of text, no "Let that sink in", no "Agree?", no "Read that again", no "Here's the thing", no emoji bullets. Ryan's writing reads like plain, direct paragraphs.
Zero emoji anywhere in a post, caption, hashtag, or slide.

Never reference a specific year or a month-year string. Use durations instead ("in 11 months", "over two and a half years"). "During COVID" is allowed because it already appears on the live site. Never use relative-time phrasing either ("last week", "this year") since posts are scheduled weeks in advance.
example: Bad: back in 2024 we started this. Good: over the past two and a half years, we built this.

detail: Prefer "which means", "so that way", constructions that link cause to effect. Use spoken connectors like "And look", "Well", "Plus", "But honestly" sparingly to open a new beat, not to pad every sentence.
Every post must survive being read aloud in Ryan's cadence: short sentences, one longer breath-sentence per paragraph, plain English, no jargon.

Get inside the reader's head and echo their actual internal monologue rather than describing them from outside. "You're reaching for your phone before your feet hit the floor", not "founders reach for their phones early."
When correcting a false belief: name the false belief, state the truth plainly, then show the mechanism that makes it true.
